title: Word Ladder
statement: Given beginWord, endWord and a list of words, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord, where each step changes exactly one letter and every word after the first must appear in the word list. Return 0 if no such sequence exists. All words have the same length.
realWorld: Spell correction and fuzzy matching pipelines: given a typo and a known-good token, find the shortest chain of single-character edits through valid dictionary entries. The same shape appears in staged migrations, where each intermediate configuration must itself be a deployable one, and you want the fewest hops between two valid states.

examples.explanation: hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog is five words. hit -> hot -> lot -> log -> cog is another five-word route; there is none shorter.
endWord is not in the list, so no sequence can legally end on it. Every word after the first must be a list word.
Single-letter words: a -> c directly. The answer counts words, not edits, so a one-edit hop is 2.

constraints: All words are lowercase English letters and the list has no duplicates
beginWord may or may not be in wordList

complexity.time: O(n^2 * L) to build the graph, O(n^2) to search it
complexity.space: O(n^2) for the adjacency list in the worst case

bruteForce.whySlow: The BFS itself is fine; the graph construction is the waste. n(n-1)/2 pairs are compared and almost all of them fail on the second differing character — with 5000 words that is 12.5 million comparisons to discover a few thousand edges. Worse, the comparison answers a question we never needed to ask pairwise: we do not care which words are adjacent to each other in general, only which words are adjacent to a word we are currently holding, and that can be derived from the word itself.

patternIdentification: Two signals stack here. First, 'shortest sequence' with every step costing the same is BFS, because BFS reaches nodes in order of distance and so the first arrival at a node is provably its shortest. Second, and easier to miss: nobody handed you a graph. The nodes are words, the edges are 'differs in one letter', and neither is written down anywhere. Whenever states are generated by a rule instead of listed, you have an implicit graph — traverse it by generating neighbours on demand and never materialise it. Once you see that, the only real design question left is how to generate the neighbours of a word cheaply.

optimized.idea: Preprocess the dictionary into wildcard buckets: for every word and every position, file the word under the pattern with that position replaced by '*', so 'hot', 'hat' and 'hit' all land in the bucket 'h*t'. Two words are neighbours exactly when they share a bucket. Building the buckets costs O(n * L^2) (L patterns per word, each L characters to construct), and looking up a word's neighbours is L bucket reads instead of n comparisons. Then run ordinary level-by-level BFS, counting words rather than edges. The further optimisation is bidirectional BFS: expand from beginWord and endWord alternately, always the smaller frontier, and stop when they meet. It roughly square-roots the explored frontier, but it is genuinely harder to get right - you need two visited maps, you must swap frontiers deliberately, and the meet condition is checked when a newly generated word appears in the *other* side's visited set, which is off by one from where people usually put it. Write the single-directional version first and only reach for it when the frontier is actually the bottleneck.

commonMistakes: Starting the counter at 0 and returning the number of edits rather than the number of words — example 1 comes back as 4 instead of 5, and the single-letter example 3 as 1 instead of 2.

Marking a word visited when it is dequeued instead of when it is enqueued — 'dot' and 'lot' both discover 'log', so it enters the queue twice and the duplication compounds level by level; the answer is still right, which is why this shows up only as a timeout on the 5000-word tests.

Building the wildcard key with word.replace(word.charAt(i), '*') instead of substring concatenation — replace() rewrites every occurrence of that character, so 'noon' at position 1 becomes 'n**n' rather than 'n*on'. Words with repeated letters silently lose their neighbours and the search returns 0 on inputs that plainly have an answer.
